''agrimonia'', a false reading of ''argemonia'' (Pliny), a plant similar to another called ''argemōne'' (Pliny), < Gr. ἀργεμώνη, a certain plant, < ἄργεμον, also ἄργεμα, a white speck in the eye, for which this plant is said to have been regarded as a cure, < ἀργός, white, shining.] The general name of plants of the genus ''Agrimonia'', natural order ''Rosaceæ'', which includes several

species of the northern hemisphere and South America. {{smaller|They are perennial herbs, with pinnate leaves, yellow flowers, and a rigid calyx-tube beset above with hooked bristles. The common agrimony, ''A. Eupatoria'', of Europe and the United States, was formerly of much repute in medicine. Its leaves and root-stock are astringent, and the latter yields a yellow dye.}}

'''agrin''' (a-grin′), ''prep. phr.'' as ''adv.'' or ''a.'' [< ''a''<sup>3</sup> + ''grin.''] In the act or state of grinning; on the grin: as, “his visage all ''agrin,''” ''Tennyson.''

'''agriological''' (ag″ri-ọ̄-loj′i-kạl), ''a.'' Of or pertaining to agriology.

'''agriologist''' (ag-ri-ol′ọ̄-jist), ''n.'' [< ''agriology'' + ''-ist.''] One who makes a comparative study of human customs, especially of the customs of man in a rude or uncivilized state. ''Max Müller.''

'''agriology''' (ag-ri-ol′ọ̄-ji), ''n.'' [< Gr. ἄγριος, wild, savage (< ἀγρός, field), + -λογία, < λέγειν, speak: see ''-ology''.] The comparative study of the customs of man in his uncivilized state.

'''Agrion''' (ag′ri-on), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἄγριος, living in the fields, < ἀγρός, a field.] The typical genus of the family ''Agrionidæ'' or group ''Agrionina''. ''A. saucium'' is red, variegated with black.

'''agrionid''' (ag-ri-on′id), ''n.'' A dragon-fly of the family ''Agrionidæ''.

'''Agrionidæ''' (ag-ri-on′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Agrion'' + ''-idæ''.] A family of neuropterous insects, or dragon-flies, closely related to the ''Libellulidæ'', of the group ''Odonata'', order ''Neuroptera'': named from a leading genus, ''Agrion'', a species of which, ''A. puella'', is the common blue dragon-fly of Britain.

'''Agrionina''' (ag″ri-ọ̄-nī′nä̤), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Agrion'' + ''-ina''.] A group of dragon-flies, typified by the genus ''Agrion'' and corresponding to the family ''Agrionidæ'', comprising small slender-bodied forms with metallic hues, whose larvæ have external leaf-like gills.

'''agriopodid''' (ag-ri-op′ọ̄-did), ''n.'' A fish of the family ''Agriopodidæ''.

'''Agriopodidæ''' (ag″ri-ọ̄-pod′i-dē), ''n. pl.'' [NL., < ''Agriopus'' (''-pod-'') + ''-idæ''.] A family of acanthopterygian fishes, represented by the genus ''Agri-''

It includes those ''Cottoidea'' in which the dorsal fin is very long, commencing on the nape, and consisting of an elongated acanthopterous and short arthropterous portion; the anal fin is short; the ventrals are thoracic and well developed, and have 1 spine and 5 soft rays; the head is compressed, with small mouth and lateral eyes; the branchial apertures are separated by an isthmus; the trunk is nuchadiform and compressed; and the vertebræ are numerous (for example, 18 abdominal and 21 caudal).}}

'''agriot''', ''n.'' See ''egriot''.

'''Agriotes''' (a-grī′ọ-tēz), ''n.'' [NL., < Gr. ἀγριότης, wildness, < ἄγριος, wild, < ἀγρός, field.] A genus of coleopterous insects, of the family ''Elateridæ'' (click-beetles or snapping-beetles), of the pentamerous division of the order ''Coleoptera''. {{smaller|The larvæ of several species, as the British ''A. lineatus'', are well known as wire-worms. See cut under ''wire-worm''.}}

'''agrippa''' (a-grip′ä̤), ''n.''; pl. ''agrippæ'' (-ē). [NL. Cf. L. ''Agrippa'', a Roman family name.] In ''obstet.'': (''a'') A person born with the feet foremost. (''b'') Foot-presentation; a footling case.

'''Agrippinian''' (ag-ri-pin′i-a̤n), ''n.'' [< LL. ''Agrippiniani'', pl., < ''Agrippinus'', a personal name, < L. ''Agrippa'', a Roman family name.] ''Eccles.'', a follower of Agrippinus, bishop of Carthage, probably late in the second century, who taught that apostates should be rebaptized.

'''agrise†''', ''v.'' [< ME. ''agrisen'' (sometimes misspelled ''agrysen''), pret. ''agros'', shudder, be terrified, < AS. ''āgrīsan'', pret. *''āgrās'', shudder, be terrified, < ''ā-'' + *''grīsan'', > early ME. ''grisen'', pret. ''gros'', shudder, be terrified: see ''grisly''.] '''I.''' ''trans.'' '''1.''' To cause to shudder or tremble; terrify; disgust.
{{smaller block|<poem>All where was nothing heard but hideous cries,
And pitious plaints, that did the harts ''agrise''.</poem>
{{right|''Sylvester'', tr. of Du Bartas.}}}}
'''2.''' To abhor. ''Chaucer.''—'''3.''' To make frightful; disfigure.
{{smaller block|Engrost with mud which did them fowle ''agrise''.
{{right|''Spenser'', F. Q., II. vi. 46.}}}}

'''II.''' ''intrans.'' To shudder; tremble with fear; be much moved.
